rv.q: Potent drama giving a voice to British-Pakistani women caught up in a scandal
The evening promises more urgency than it delivers. Still, not expendable.
Intelligent but sometimes heavy-handed drama about two estranged Muslim sisters who become caught up in a grooming scandal.

With its firm criticism of fundamentalist ideas, its disgust with hypocrisy, antagonism to the far right, and its emotional commitment to change, this is a superbly intense mix of the personal and political.
Quality performances mean there is much to enjoy in this sombre, thought-provoking piece.
This ambitious, impassioned show has a lot of potential, but struggles to bring its ideas to life in a way that makes good theatre.

The strongest moments occur as we see the estranged sisters gradually moving closer, slowly mending their fragmented relationship as they unite in their desire to find ways to challenge their community and seek help.
Themes and backstories dangle, unresolved, when the lights go down.
My only difficulty was that I wanted the writer to peel back even more layers.
Hussain's writing brings most of the characters to life.

cn.t: Hussain's well-intentioned exploration of the Rotherham grooming scandal through a Pakistani family's perspective earns praise for its bold subject matter and hyper-realistic design, but critics find the execution uneven and themes underexplored.
